questions.stem: A 22 year old man has a 7 month history of low back pain that wakes him in the early hours. He is stiff for over an hour each morning and feels better after a run. He also has pain at the back of his left heel and is tired all the time. He has had no recent infections, rashes or bowel upset.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Inflammatory back pain (night pain, morning stiffness over 30 minutes, better with exercise) plus Achilles enthesitis and fatigue in a young man is AS.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.

clues: wakes him in the early hours
stiff for over an hour each morning
pain at the back of his left heel
steps.x: Night pain, **long morning stiffness** and pain that **improves with exercise** = inflammatory back pain. Heel pain = Achilles **enthesitis**. Fatigue is an important AS symptom.

elim: Widespread pain and fatigue, but not inflammatory back pain that eases with exercise or heel enthesitis.
Mechanical pain worse with activity, often with sciatica; it does not cause prolonged morning stiffness.
Worse with activity and better with rest, the opposite of his pattern.
Needs a preceding GU or GI infection and usually an asymmetrical lower limb arthritis; he has had none.

steps.x: **A. Ankylosing spondylitis.** Young man + inflammatory back pain + enthesitis = AS. No preceding infection makes reactive arthritis unlikely.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man has 8 months of low back pain and stiffness that is worst first thing in the morning and eases with activity. Two marks are drawn 10 cm above and 5 cm below the lumbosacral junction while he stands upright. He then bends forward as far as he can.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on this examination?
o: Normal increase in distance of 7 cm
Pain reproduced in the buttock at 40 degrees of leg raising
Reduced internal rotation of both hips
Schober's distance increases by only 3 cm
questions.e: This is Schober's test; an increase under 5 cm shows reduced lumbar forward flexion, as seen in AS.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on this examination? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.

clues: 10 cm above and 5 cm below the lumbosacral junction
bends forward as far as he can
steps.x: Marks above and below the lumbosacral junction, then forward flexion = **Schober's test**. With inflammatory back pain, expect it to be **reduced**.

elim: A normal result; a rise of 5 cm or more is expected in a healthy spine.
That is a positive straight leg raise for nerve root irritation, a different test.
Tests hip flexor strength and pain, not lumbar flexion.
A hip osteoarthritis sign; it does not measure lumbar flexion.

steps.x: **E. Schober's distance increases by only 3 cm.** Schober's test under 5 cm of increase suggests AS (reduced lumbar flexion).

questions.stem: A 33 year old man with ankylosing spondylitis has a 2 day history of a painful, red left eye with blurred vision and pain on looking at bright lights. His visual acuity is reduced to 6/18 in the left eye. The redness is most marked around the edge of the cornea and the pupil is small.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on slit-lamp examination?
questions.e: Painful red eye with photophobia, reduced acuity, ciliary flush and small pupil in AS is anterior uveitis; pus in the anterior chamber (hypopyon) is its complication.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on slit-lamp examination? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.

clues: pain on looking at bright lights
most marked around the edge of the cornea
steps.x: AS + painful red eye + photophobia + ciliary flush + small pupil = **anterior uveitis** (iritis).

elim: A sign of chronic glaucoma, which is painless and not red.
Herpes simplex keratitis; it is not linked to AS and stains with fluorescein as a branching ulcer.
Bacterial conjunctivitis: no photophobia and vision is preserved.
A painless flat red patch with normal vision.

steps.x: **C. Hypopyon in the anterior chamber.** Anterior uveitis is an 'A' of AS; severe cases show a hypopyon (pus in the anterior chamber).

questions.stem: A 59 year old man with ankylosing spondylitis for 30 years has had two episodes of light-headedness this week. He has had no chest pain and takes no rate-limiting drugs. His pulse rate is 38 bpm and regular, BP 118/70 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: P waves and QRS complexes are dissociated with a slow regular escape rhythm: complete heart block.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: AV node block is one of the 'A's of AS; P waves and QRS complexes are dissociated with a slow regular escape rhythm, which is complete heart block.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.

clues: pulse rate is 38 bpm and regular
steps.x: Long-standing AS + slow regular pulse + light-headedness: think **AV node block**, one of the 'A's of AS.

elim: Irregularly irregular with no P waves; his pulse is regular.
PR is prolonged but every P is conducted, so the rate is not this slow.
PR lengthens then a beat drops; P waves and QRS stay linked.
Every P is followed by a QRS at a fixed PR interval.

steps.x: **B. Complete heart block.** P waves and QRS complexes march independently = complete heart block, a cardiac complication of AS.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man with long-standing ankylosing spondylitis has 18 months of slowly worsening breathlessness on exertion. He has never smoked, has no cough or weight loss and worked as a teacher. His temperature is 36.8°C and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Chest X-ray (see item resources).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of these findings?
o: Apical fibrosis due to ankylosing spondylitis
questions.e: Bilateral upper zone fibrosis in long-standing AS is apical fibrosis, one of the 'A's; asbestosis and IPF are lower zone.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of these findings? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.

clues: never smoked, has no cough or weight loss
steps.x: Long-standing AS + slowly worsening breathlessness + no infection or exposure: think of the 'A's.

elim: Causes LOWER zone fibrosis and needs asbestos exposure; he was a teacher.
Typically basal and peripheral, not apical.
Can cause upper zone change, but expect cough, weight loss or fever.
Shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, often in younger adults.

steps.x: **A. Apical fibrosis due to ankylosing spondylitis.** Upper zone fibrosis: think AS (apical fibrosis), TB, sarcoid. Lower zone: IPF, asbestosis.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man has had poorly controlled ankylosing spondylitis for 28 years. He now has 2 months of swollen ankles and frothy urine. His BP is 128/80 mmHg. He takes no regular medicines other than paracetamol.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his renal disease?
questions.e: Decades of uncontrolled inflammation deposit serum amyloid A in the kidney, causing nephrotic syndrome; amyloidosis is one of the 'A's of AS.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of his renal disease? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.

clues: poorly controlled ankylosing spondylitis for 28 years
steps.x: Long, uncontrolled inflammatory disease + nephrotic picture (oedema, frothy urine, low albumin, heavy proteinuria) = **AA amyloidosis**.

elim: Usually visible haematuria soon after an upper respiratory infection, not long-standing inflammation with nephrotic syndrome.
Mostly a childhood cause of nephrotic syndrome.
He is not taking an NSAID, and interstitial nephritis gives AKI rather than heavy proteinuria.
Nephritic, with haematuria and hypertension after a throat infection.

steps.x: **E. Renal AA amyloidosis.** Chronic inflammation (AS, RA) + nephrotic syndrome = AA amyloid.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has had ankylosing spondylitis for 35 years. He has a fixed stooped posture and cannot look at the horizon without bending his knees. His chest expansion is 1 cm and he has almost no movement in his lumbar spine.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on lumbar spine X-ray?
o: Collapse of one vertebra with a lytic lesion
Disc space narrowing with large osteophytes
Slip of L5 on S1 with a pars defect
Vertebral bodies bridged by syndesmophytes (bamboo spine)
questions.e: Late AS fuses the spine: syndesmophytes bridge the vertebral bodies to give a bamboo spine, matching his fixed stooped posture.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on lumbar spine X-ray? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.

clues: almost no movement in his lumbar spine
steps.x: 35 years of disease and a **fixed stooped posture** = late AS. Expect **spinal fusion**.

elim: Suggests metastasis or myeloma, not long-standing AS.
Degenerative spondylosis; osteophytes grow outward, not as thin vertical bridges.
After 35 years with a fixed stooped spine, changes are expected.
Spondylolisthesis; not the result of chronic enthesitis.

steps.x: **E. Vertebral bodies bridged by syndesmophytes (bamboo spine).** Bamboo spine is a LATE sign; sacroiliitis comes first.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man sees his GP with 5 months of low back pain. He is otherwise well with no weight loss or fever. Neurological examination of the legs is normal. The GP wants to decide whether his pain is inflammatory or mechanical.
questions.q: Which feature of his history would most suggest inflammatory back pain?
o: Pain that began after lifting a heavy box
Pain that improves with exercise and worsens with rest
Pain that is worst at the end of the working day
Stiffness that settles within 10 minutes of waking
questions.e: Inflammatory back pain improves with exercise and worsens with rest, with morning stiffness over 30 minutes; mechanical pain is the reverse.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which feature of his history would most suggest inflammatory back pain? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.
Chronic back pain in a young man: the question is the **pattern**. Inflammatory pain = better with movement, worse at rest, long morning stiffness.

elim: Suggests nerve root irritation from a disc, not inflammation.
A mechanical trigger.
Mechanical pain builds with use through the day.
Inflammatory morning stiffness lasts more than 30 minutes.

steps.x: **C. Pain that improves with exercise and worsens with rest.** Better with exercise, worse at rest, stiffness over 30 minutes = inflammatory (think AS).

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman has 1 year of low back stiffness lasting about an hour each morning, and pain under both heels on first standing. Two years ago she was treated in eye casualty for a painful red eye. She has no rash, mouth ulcers or diarrhoea. Her CRP is 24 mg/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Inflammatory back pain, plantar enthesitis and previous anterior uveitis with a raised CRP point to AS, which also affects women.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.

clues: low back stiffness lasting about an hour each morning
pain under both heels on first standing
steps.x: Inflammatory back stiffness + heel **enthesitis** + previous **uveitis** = spondyloarthropathy. No infection, rash or bowel upset.

elim: Inflammatory markers are normal and there is no eye inflammation.
Affects people over 50 with shoulder and hip girdle stiffness.
Symmetrical small joint hand arthritis; it causes scleritis, not uveitis.
Expect rash, mouth ulcers and arthralgia rather than enthesitis and spinal stiffness.

steps.x: **A. Ankylosing spondylitis.** AS is commoner in men but not only in men; uveitis + enthesitis + inflammatory back pain = AS.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man has had ankylosing spondylitis for 20 years, treated with naproxen. He has never taken corticosteroids, drinks little alcohol and does not smoke. A routine DEXA scan shows a lumbar spine T-score of −2.7.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his low bone density?
questions.e: Chronic inflammation in AS raises the risk of osteoporosis and fragility fractures; the other causes are excluded by his history and bloods.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of his low bone density? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.
Osteoporosis in a middle-aged man with no steroids and normal bloods: the cause is the **disease itself**.

elim: His testosterone is normal.
He has never taken corticosteroids.
Calcium and PTH are normal.
His vitamin D level is normal.

steps.x: **D. Systemic inflammation from ankylosing spondylitis.** AS inflammation causes osteoporosis, so NICE suggests screening every 2 years.

questions.stem: A 31 year old man with 3 years of inflammatory back pain is examined in rheumatology clinic. His lungs are clear on auscultation and percussion. His oxygen saturation is 98% breathing air and his chest X-ray is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on chest examination?
o: Dullness to percussion at one base
questions.e: Enthesitis at the costovertebral and costochondral joints reduces chest expansion in AS, even with clear lungs.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on chest examination? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.
Inflammatory back pain = AS. A clear chest and normal X-ray mean the sign is **mechanical**, not in the lung.

elim: His lungs are clear on auscultation.
His lungs are resonant and his X-ray is normal.
He has no airways disease, and his chest is clear.
There is no effusion, collapse or pneumothorax on his X-ray.

steps.x: **D. Reduced chest expansion.** AS signs: reduced chest expansion, reduced lateral lumbar flexion (early), Schober's under 5 cm, stooped posture (late).

questions.stem: A 24 year old man attends eye casualty with a painful red right eye and photophobia. Slit-lamp examination confirms anterior uveitis. On questioning, he has 6 months of low back and buttock pain that wakes him at night and is better after exercise. He has no mouth or genital ulcers.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.e: Anterior uveitis with inflammatory back and buttock pain in a young man is AS; the HLA-B27 and IL-17/IL-23 links explain the association.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely underlying diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.

clues: low back and buttock pain that wakes him at night
steps.x: Uveitis + inflammatory back pain + buttock pain (sacroiliitis) in a young man = **AS**.

elim: Uveitis with recurrent mouth and genital ulcers; he has neither.
Causes episcleritis or scleritis with symmetrical small joint arthritis.
Can cause uveitis but not inflammatory back and buttock pain.
Causes dry, gritty eyes, not acute anterior uveitis.

steps.x: **A. Ankylosing spondylitis.** Young man with anterior uveitis: ask about the back. AS shares the HLA-B27 pathway with uveitis.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man with ankylosing spondylitis has 3 weeks of pain at the back of his right heel, worst in the morning. There is tenderness and swelling where the tendon inserts into the calcaneus. The first metatarsophalangeal joint is normal and he has not changed his exercise routine.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his heel pain?
questions.e: Inflammation where the Achilles tendon inserts into bone is enthesitis, a hallmark of AS.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of his heel pain? Decide what kind of answer it wants (a diagnosis, finding or cause) before reading the options.

clues: where the tendon inserts into the calcaneus
steps.x: Pain and swelling at a tendon **insertion into bone** in AS = **enthesitis**.

elim: Follows a sharp increase in training load; his routine has not changed.
Classically the first MTP joint, which is normal.
A painful skin lesion on the sole, not at the tendon insertion.
Nerve entrapment causing burning and tingling in the sole.

steps.x: **B. Enthesitis of the Achilles insertion.** AS inflames entheses: Achilles tendonitis, plantar fasciitis, costochondritis.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man has 1 year of inflammatory low back pain and alternating buttock pain. His GP arranges an X-ray of the pelvis. The radiologist reports a finding that would fulfil the modified New York classification criteria for ankylosing spondylitis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reported finding?
o: Joint space narrowing of both hips with osteophytes
questions.e: Radiographic sacroiliitis is the most specific X-ray sign and is needed to meet the modified New York criteria.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely reported finding? It wants a test (or a test result). Decide which test, and why, before reading the options.
Alternating buttock pain = **sacroiliac joints**. The modified New York criteria hinge on **radiographic sacroiliitis**.

elim: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition, seen in pseudogout.
Hip osteoarthritis.
A finding in the hands and feet in psoriatic arthritis, not on a pelvic film.
Seen after trauma or pregnancy.

steps.x: **D. Sacroiliitis on both sides.** Pelvic X-ray first; sacroiliitis is the key finding for the modified New York criteria.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man has had ankylosing spondylitis for 6 years. A lateral X-ray of his lumbar spine is taken to look for spinal involvement. He still has some lumbar movement and no fixed deformity. His CRP has been persistently raised and his pelvic X-ray shows sacroiliitis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on this X-ray?
o: Loss of the pedicle (winking owl sign)
questions.e: Erosion at the corners of the vertebral bodies in AS gives squaring; syndesmophytes and bamboo spine follow later.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on this X-ray? It wants a test (or a test result). Decide which test, and why, before reading the options.

clues: lateral X-ray of his lumbar spine
steps.x: AS for 6 years with **no fixed deformity**: earlier spinal change, not yet bamboo spine.

elim: Biconcave vertebrae of osteoporosis or sickle cell disease.
Dense single vertebra in Paget's disease, lymphoma or metastasis.
Suggests metastatic destruction.
Thickened cortex in Paget's disease.

steps.x: **E. Squaring of the vertebral bodies.** AS spine X-ray: squaring, then syndesmophytes, then bamboo spine (late).

questions.stem: A 38 year old man has 8 years of inflammatory back pain and is HLA-B27 positive. A plain X-ray of his sacroiliac joints is taken in clinic. His CRP is 19 mg/L and his ESR is 34 mm/hr.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on this X-ray?
o: Normal sacroiliac joints with hip osteophytes
Subchondral erosions and sclerosis of both sacroiliac joints
Unilateral sacroiliac joint widening after a fall
questions.e: Long-standing sacroiliitis shows erosions and sclerosis either side of the SI joint, then fusion.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on this X-ray? It wants a test (or a test result). Decide which test, and why, before reading the options.
Long-standing, active, HLA-B27-positive inflammatory back pain = AS with established **sacroiliitis**.

elim: Chondrocalcinosis of the knee in pseudogout.
After 8 years of active disease, the SI joints are expected to show change.
Gouty tophi erosions.
Trauma, not chronic inflammation.

steps.x: **D. Subchondral erosions and sclerosis of both sacroiliac joints.** SI joint X-ray in AS: subchondral erosions and sclerosis, then fusion.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man has 3 months of low back pain that wakes him at 4 am and improves when he gets up and moves. He is stiff for 45 minutes each morning. His CRP is 15 mg/L. X-ray of the pelvis shows normal sacroiliac joints.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: MRI of the sacroiliac joints is the gold standard and detects early sacroiliitis (bone marrow oedema) long before X-ray change.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation? It wants a test (or a test result). Decide which test, and why, before reading the options.

clues: X-ray of the pelvis shows normal sacroiliac joints
steps.x: Early disease (**3 months**) with a **normal X-ray**: X-ray sacroiliitis appears late.

elim: Shows bone but misses early bone marrow oedema, and gives a high radiation dose to a young man.
Supports but cannot confirm AS; many healthy people carry it.
X-ray change appears only after years, not in a week.
Non-specific and less sensitive than MRI.

steps.x: **C. MRI of the sacroiliac joints.** Suspected early AS with a normal X-ray: MRI of the SI joints.

questions.stem: A 32 year old woman with ankylosing spondylitis has persistent pain and swelling at the back of both heels despite naproxen. Her rheumatologist wants to assess how much active inflammation there is at the tendon insertions before changing her treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: Ultrasound of the Achilles tendon insertions
questions.e: Ultrasound is the second-line test to assess the severity of inflammation and enthesitis at affected sites.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation? It wants a test (or a test result). Decide which test, and why, before reading the options.

clues: pain and swelling at the back of both heels
how much active inflammation there is at the tendon insertions
steps.x: She wants to see **active inflammation at the tendon insertions** (enthesitis) now, so pick a soft tissue imaging test.

elim: Test for neuropathy, not tendon inflammation.
Shows late bony change, not current soft tissue inflammation.
A genetic marker; it says nothing about current inflammation.
Used for gout, not enthesitis.

steps.x: **D. Ultrasound of the Achilles tendon insertions.** Ultrasound grades enthesitis and joint inflammation in AS.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man with ankylosing spondylitis had a normal DEXA scan at his last review. He asks how often his bone density should be checked, as his brother with the same condition had a spinal fracture.
questions.q: According to NICE, how often should he be screened for osteoporosis?
questions.e: NICE recommends osteoporosis screening every 2 years in AS, because chronic inflammation raises the risk of fragility fractures.

steps.x: The lead-in is: According to NICE, how often should he be screened for osteoporosis? It wants a test (or a test result). Decide which test, and why, before reading the options.

clues: how often his bone density should be checked
steps.x: AS causes **osteoporosis** through chronic inflammation; NICE sets a fixed screening interval.

elim: Too infrequent for the NICE AS recommendation.
More often than recommended; bone density changes slowly.
Screening aims to find osteoporosis BEFORE a fracture.
The AS inflammation itself raises the risk, steroids or not.

steps.x: **A. Every 2 years.** AS: DEXA every 2 years (NICE).

questions.stem: A 23 year old man has 6 months of inflammatory low back pain. In clinic, the doctor wants a simple bedside measurement of his lumbar forward flexion that can be repeated at each visit to follow his disease.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate test?
questions.e: Schober's test measures lumbar flexion; an increase under 5 cm suggests AS and can be tracked over time.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate test? It wants a test (or a test result). Decide which test, and why, before reading the options.
A bedside measure of **lumbar forward flexion** in suspected AS has a name.

elim: Stresses the hip and sacroiliac joint to provoke pain; it does not measure flexion.
Tests for sciatic nerve root irritation.
Detects a fixed flexion deformity of the hip.
Tests hip abductor weakness.

steps.x: **B. Schober's test.** Schober's test: increase under 5 cm = reduced lumbar flexion, suggesting AS.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man has just been diagnosed with ankylosing spondylitis. His GP starts naproxen. He works in an office, sits most of the day and has stopped going to the gym because of pain. He asks what else he can do himself to keep his spine moving and reduce stiffness.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate addition to his treatment?
questions.e: First-line AS treatment is an NSAID plus a physiotherapy and exercise programme to keep spinal mobility.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate addition to his treatment? It wants an action. Decide what you would actually do next before reading the options.

clues: just been diagnosed with ankylosing spondylitis
steps.x: New AS: first-line is **NSAID + exercise**. He is on the NSAID; what is missing?

elim: Rest makes inflammatory pain and stiffness WORSE.
Systemic steroids are not used for axial AS.
Not first-line treatment; exercise is.
Immobilisation worsens stiffness and posture.

steps.x: **D. Physiotherapy-led exercise programme.** AS first-line = NSAID (ibuprofen/naproxen) + physiotherapy/exercise.

questions.stem: A 21 year old man has 9 months of inflammatory back pain. MRI shows active bilateral sacroiliitis and he is diagnosed with ankylosing spondylitis. He has no history of peptic ulcer, asthma or kidney disease. His eGFR is above 90 mL/min.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial drug treatment?
questions.e: NSAIDs such as naproxen or ibuprofen, with exercise, are first-line in AS; biologics come only after NSAIDs fail.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial drug treatment? It wants an action. Decide what you would actually do next before reading the options.

clues: no history of peptic ulcer, asthma or kidney disease
steps.x: Newly diagnosed AS with **no contraindication to NSAIDs** = start an NSAID.

elim: A TNF-alpha inhibitor reserved for when NSAIDs have failed.
Has no proven benefit in axial AS.
Systemic steroids are not first-line in AS.
An IL-17 inhibitor used when TNF inhibitors are unsuitable.

steps.x: **B. Naproxen.** AS ladder: NSAID + exercise, then TNF-alpha inhibitor, then IL-17 inhibitor.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man with ankylosing spondylitis has had persistent back pain and morning stiffness despite 4 weeks each of two different NSAIDs at full dose and a regular exercise programme. His disease activity score remains high. Screening for TB and hepatitis is negative.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: When NSAIDs fail, a TNF-alpha inhibitor (etanercept, adalimumab or infliximab) is the next step; conventional DMARDs do not help spinal disease.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? It wants an action. Decide what you would actually do next before reading the options.

clues: despite 4 weeks each of two different NSAIDs
Screening for TB and hepatitis is negative
steps.x: Two NSAIDs have failed and he has been **screened for TB**: that is preparation for a **biologic**.

elim: An RA/lupus DMARD with no role in axial AS.
Ineffective for axial disease.
Systemic steroids are not used for axial AS.
May help peripheral arthritis but not axial spinal disease.

steps.x: **A. Etanercept.** NSAIDs failed in AS = TNF-alpha inhibitor (etanercept, adalimumab, infliximab).

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman with ankylosing spondylitis has active spinal disease despite two NSAIDs and physiotherapy. Her BASDAI score is 6.5. She also has multiple sclerosis diagnosed 4 years ago, so her rheumatologist advises against TNF-alpha inhibitors. Screening for TB is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: If TNF-alpha inhibitors are unsuitable, an IL-17 inhibitor (secukinumab) is used instead.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate treatment? It wants an action. Decide what you would actually do next before reading the options.
NSAIDs failed, but **TNF inhibitors are unsuitable**: the alternative biologic class.

elim: A TNF-alpha inhibitor, which is unsuitable here (it can worsen demyelinating disease).
Also a TNF-alpha inhibitor, so has the same problem.
An RA DMARD without benefit in axial AS.
Not used to control axial AS.

steps.x: **E. Secukinumab.** Biologic for AS when TNF-alpha inhibitors are unsuitable = IL-17 inhibitor (secukinumab).

questions.stem: A 35 year old man with ankylosing spondylitis is seen in eye casualty with 3 days of severe pain, redness and photophobia in his left eye. Slit-lamp examination shows severe anterior uveitis with a 2 mm hypopyon. Intraocular pressure is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Severe uveitis or hypopyon is treated with topical cyclopentolate (a mydriatic that relieves ciliary spasm), usually alongside topical steroid, under ophthalmology.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate treatment? It wants an action. Decide what you would actually do next before reading the options.

clues: severe anterior uveitis with a 2 mm hypopyon
steps.x: AS + **severe anterior uveitis with hypopyon** = treat the inflammation and ciliary spasm.

elim: For dry eyes; it does nothing for severe uveitis.
For herpes zoster or herpes simplex eye infection.
Treats bacterial conjunctivitis; a hypopyon here is sterile inflammation.
Lowers raised intraocular pressure in glaucoma; his pressure is normal.

steps.x: **D. Topical cyclopentolate.** Severe uveitis/hypopyon in AS: topical cyclopentolate (plus steroid drops) under ophthalmology.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man with ankylosing spondylitis is seen in rheumatology clinic for a routine review. He mentions his right eye became painful and red this morning, his vision is slightly blurred and bright lights hurt. His back pain is well controlled on naproxen.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: An acute painful red eye with photophobia and blurred vision in AS suggests anterior uveitis, which needs urgent same-day ophthalmology assessment.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? It wants an action. Decide what you would actually do next before reading the options.

clues: vision is slightly blurred and bright lights hurt
steps.x: AS + **painful red eye + photophobia + blurred vision** = anterior uveitis until proven otherwise.

elim: This will not treat the eye.
Treats bacterial conjunctivitis; this painful, photophobic eye is uveitis.
Too slow; untreated uveitis can damage vision.
Biologic escalation is for uncontrolled disease, not the emergency step for an acute eye.

steps.x: **D. Same-day referral to ophthalmology.** Red painful eye in AS = same-day ophthalmology.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man with ankylosing spondylitis has a DEXA scan as part of his regular screening. His femoral neck T-score is −2.8. He has had no fractures. His calcium, vitamin D and renal function are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management of his bone density?
o: No treatment until he has a fracture
Oral alendronate with calcium and vitamin D
Repeat DEXA in 2 years without treatment
questions.e: A T-score of −2.5 or below is osteoporosis; AS raises fracture risk, so a bisphosphonate with calcium and vitamin D is the standard UK treatment.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate management of his bone density? It wants an action. Decide what you would actually do next before reading the options.
T-score **−2.8** = osteoporosis. AS already raises fracture risk; treat before a fracture.

elim: Used in postmenopausal women, not men.
The aim is to prevent fragility fractures.
Steroids worsen bone loss.
He already has osteoporosis (T-score −2.5 or below), so he needs treatment now.

steps.x: **C. Oral alendronate with calcium and vitamin D.** AS-related osteoporosis: bisphosphonate (alendronate) plus calcium and vitamin D.

questions.stem: A 20 year old man has 6 months of inflammatory low back pain and buttock pain. His father had a 'fused spine' and needed a walking stick by 50. MRI shows bilateral sacroiliitis. His rheumatoid factor is negative.
questions.q: Which genetic marker is he most likely to carry?
questions.e: AS is strongly associated with HLA-B27; family history and male sex are risk factors.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which genetic marker is he most likely to carry? It wants a mechanism. Say the mechanism in your own words before reading the options.
Family history of spinal fusion + sacroiliitis + RF negative = **seronegative spondyloarthropathy** (AS).

elim: Linked to Behçet's disease.
Linked to coeliac disease.
Linked to type 1 diabetes, SLE and Graves' disease.
Linked to rheumatoid arthritis.

steps.x: **A. HLA-B27.** AS = HLA-B27. RA = HLA-DR4. Behçet's = HLA-B51.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man with HLA-B27 positive ankylosing spondylitis has back pain, Achilles tendon pain and plantar fasciitis. His medical student sister asks which tissue is the main site of inflammation in his disease, unlike in rheumatoid arthritis.
questions.q: Which is the primary site of inflammation?
o: Entheses (tendon and ligament insertions into bone)
questions.e: In AS, HLA-B27 is thought to trigger autoimmune inflammation at the entheses rather than the synovium, explaining Achilles tendonitis and plantar fasciitis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the primary site of inflammation? It wants a mechanism. Say the mechanism in your own words before reading the options.

clues: Achilles tendon pain and plantar fasciitis
steps.x: Achilles tendon and plantar fascia pain both arise at **insertions into bone**. RA targets the synovium.

elim: Cartilage loss is a feature of osteoarthritis, not the primary target in AS.
Disc degeneration is mechanical, not AS inflammation.
Muscle inflammation is myositis.
The primary target in rheumatoid arthritis, not AS.

steps.x: **B. Entheses (tendon and ligament insertions into bone).** AS = enthesitis; RA = synovitis.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man has had ankylosing spondylitis for 25 years. His spine X-ray shows thin vertical bony bridges joining adjacent vertebral bodies along the length of his lumbar spine, and his spine is now almost immobile.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of these changes?
o: Bone marrow infiltration by plasma cells
Calcium pyrophosphate deposition in the discs
Erosion at entheses followed by new bone formation (syndesmophytes)
questions.e: Chronic enthesitis erodes bone, which is then repaired by new bone (syndesmophytes) that bridges vertebral bodies into a bamboo spine.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of these changes? It wants a mechanism. Say the mechanism in your own words before reading the options.

clues: thin vertical bony bridges joining adjacent vertebral bodies
steps.x: Vertical bony bridges between vertebrae after long AS = **syndesmophytes**, forming a bamboo spine.

elim: Myeloma causes lytic lesions, not bony bridges.
Causes chondrocalcinosis, not fusion of vertebral bodies.
Osteophytes are horizontal and come from mechanical wear.
This is Paget's disease.

steps.x: **D. Erosion at entheses followed by new bone formation (syndesmophytes).** Bamboo spine = inflammation, erosion, then new bone (syndesmophytes) bridging vertebrae.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man with ankylosing spondylitis has also developed Crohn's disease and patches of psoriasis on his elbows. He has had one episode of anterior uveitis. He is otherwise well and his rheumatoid factor is negative. He asks his rheumatologist why these conditions have clustered together.
questions.q: Which shared mechanism best explains this?
o: HLA-B27 and the IL-17/IL-23 inflammatory axis
Immune complex deposition with low complement
questions.e: AS shares HLA-B27 and the IL-17/IL-23 axis with uveitis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which shared mechanism best explains this? It wants a mechanism. Say the mechanism in your own words before reading the options.

clues: Crohn's disease and patches of psoriasis
steps.x: Spondyloarthropathy + IBD + psoriasis + uveitis = one **shared genetic and cytokine pathway**.

elim: Linked to rheumatoid arthritis.
The mechanism in lupus.
NSAIDs do not cause psoriasis, Crohn's disease or uveitis.
The mechanism of gout.

steps.x: **B. HLA-B27 and the IL-17/IL-23 inflammatory axis.** AS, uveitis, psoriasis and IBD share HLA-B27 and the IL-17/IL-23 axis.

questions.stem: A 41 year old man with ankylosing spondylitis did not respond to two NSAIDs and could not have a TNF-alpha inhibitor because of recurrent infections. He is started on secukinumab and his morning stiffness improves over 3 months.
questions.q: Which is the mechanism of action of this drug?
questions.e: Secukinumab is an IL-17 inhibitor; IL-17 and TNF-alpha are the key cytokines in AS, which is why both are drug targets.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the mechanism of action of this drug? It wants a mechanism. Say the mechanism in your own words before reading the options.
Secukinumab is the AS biologic used when **TNF inhibitors are unsuitable**: an IL-17 inhibitor.

elim: This is tocilizumab, used in RA and GCA.
This is rituximab.
This is how NSAIDs work.
This is how adalimumab, etanercept and infliximab work.

steps.x: **D. Neutralises interleukin-17A.** AS biologics: TNF-alpha inhibitors first; IL-17 inhibitor (secukinumab) as the alternative.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man has inflammatory back pain, bilateral sacroiliitis on MRI and Achilles enthesitis. His rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies are both negative. He is HLA-B27 positive and has no psoriasis, bowel symptoms or recent infection. His CRP is 21 mg/L.
questions.q: Which best describes the classification of his condition?
questions.e: AS is a seronegative (RF negative) spondyloarthropathy strongly linked to HLA-B27, as are reactive and psoriatic arthritis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which best describes the classification of his condition? It wants a mechanism. Say the mechanism in your own words before reading the options.

clues: rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies are both negative
steps.x: Spine and SI joint inflammation + **RF and anti-CCP negative** + **HLA-B27** = seronegative spondyloarthropathy.

elim: Lupus and systemic sclerosis, with ANA and other autoantibodies.
Gout and pseudogout, caused by crystal deposition.
RA with positive RF or anti-CCP; his are negative.
ANCA-associated conditions affecting small vessels.

steps.x: **C. Seronegative spondyloarthropathy.** AS, reactive and psoriatic arthritis and IBD arthritis are seronegative spondyloarthropathies.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman with ankylosing spondylitis has sharp pain under her heel with the first steps each morning. There is tenderness where the plantar fascia attaches to the calcaneus. She also has tenderness over the costochondral junctions.

Crystal deposition in the subtalar joint
Inflammation at the insertion of the plantar fascia into bone
questions.e: Enthesitis rather than synovitis explains plantar fasciitis, Achilles tendonitis and costochondritis in AS.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of her heel pain? It wants a mechanism. Say the mechanism in your own words before reading the options.

steps.x: Heel pain at the **fascia attachment** plus **costochondral** tenderness: both are entheses.

Gout or pseudogout.

AS pain at these sites comes from entheses, not synovium.
